messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Michael is a 25-year-old European male who works as a salesperson in New York. He experienced significant trauma when he was caught in a war zone during his travels through Eastern Europe. Since returning home, Michael has been struggling with intense negative emotions and difficulties that have affected various aspects of his life. The traumatic event began on a seemingly normal day while Michael was walking through the streets of a small town. Suddenly, explosions shattered the calm, and gunfire erupted all around him. He found himself running for cover as buildings crumbled and people screamed in terror. The sounds and sights of that day remain vivid in his mind, replaying like a nightmarish loop whenever he closes his eyes. Since returning home, Michael has experienced overwhelming feelings of fear, horror, anger, guilt, and shame. These emotions are not just fleeting moments but persistent and intense, making it difficult for him to feel at ease even in the safety of his own home. He often finds himself questioning why he survived when others did not, leading to a deep sense of guilt. At night, Michael struggles with an increased state of vigilance that makes it nearly impossible to relax or sleep peacefully. The darkness intensifies his feelings of vulnerability and danger, and every small sound sends him into a heightened state of alertness. This constant state of night vigilance has disrupted his sleep patterns significantly, leaving him exhausted during the day. His job as a salesperson has also been affected by these symptoms. Michael’s concentration at work has noticeably declined, making it difficult for him to focus on tasks that require sustained attention. He often finds himself staring blankly at his computer screen or walking away from meetings prematurely because he cannot follow through with the conversation due to his preoccupation with intrusive thoughts about the war zone. Michael's relationship with his partner has also been impacted. Although he loves her deeply, he is not able to share the full extent of what he experienced and feels isolated by his inability to articulate his emotions. He avoids discussing his trauma because it triggers intense negative feelings that he finds hard to manage. Over time, these symptoms have led Michael to feel increasingly disconnected from the world around him. His partner notices changes in his behavior but struggles to understand the depth of his internal turmoil. Michael has come to believe that no one can truly comprehend what he went through, further isolating himself emotionally and socially. The most challenging aspect for Michael is not knowing how much longer he can endure these overwhelming feelings without significant support. What finally brought him to seek help was a realization that he cannot continue living in this state of constant fear and guilt. He hopes to find ways to manage his emotions and regain some sense of normalcy in his daily life, including the ability to focus at work and connect more deeply with his partner. Michael is most afraid that he will never be able to shake off the memories of that day and worries about becoming increasingly isolated from those who care about him. His primary hope is to find a way to process his trauma without it continuing to dominate every aspect of his life, allowing him to reconnect with others and live more fully.
